items.title: Warren Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 23, 1995
items.q: I did some jazz party and they put a bunch of trumpet players on the stand and Sweets was with us.

ctx.x: Well you really echo the sentiments of some of the other fellows we’ve talked to, Al Grey and Sweets Edison, they said the same thing in different ways.

items.title: Warren Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 23, 1995
items.q: I did some jazz party and they put a bunch of trumpet players on the stand and Sweets was with us.

ctx.x: He said the same thing: he said that he doesn’t hear, well he wasn’t complaining. He said that today he doesn’t hear that striving for sound as much as when he was coming on, and that that was a big part of everyone’s goal.

Yeah. Strength for individuality. Now everybody has a lovely, schooled, technical, marvelous approach, and I can’t distinguish one of them from another. You got three notes of Sweets, I mean Sweets Edison invented himself. He’s one of the prime characters in America and always has been. I mean it’s funny, where the hell was I, I did some jazz party and they put a bunch of trumpet players on the stand and Sweets was with us. And we’re all up there sweating and popping veins and doing our level best to impress…
How has the music scene changed for you or has it, since you started? Is it — for our aspiring jazz musicians — is it getting tougher?
